extracted.intended_audience: high-school and undergraduate students; math-contest participants and instructors studying trigonometry
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter presenting core trigonometric definitions, identities, theorems, geometric applications, and problem-solving techniques used in competition mathematics and advanced high-school/early undergraduate courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sinusoidal parameter roles
rubrics_metrics.description: For a sinusoidal function y = a sin[b(x + c)] + d, the constants a, b, c, and d play roles: a is the amplitude, b is related to the period, c is related to the horizontal shift, and d is related to the vertical shift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative matching exercises (e.g., y = sin 3x, y = 2 cos x/2, y = 3 sin 4x, y = 4 cos(x − 30°), y = 3/2 − 3, y = 2 sin[3(x + 40°)] + 5) and figure references are provided to build intuition about how each parameter affects the graph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear combination of sinusoids
rubrics_metrics.description: The linear combination af(x) + bg(x) of two sinusoidal functions f and g is sinusoidal if f and g have the same period (or frequency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text asserts the fact and leaves the proof to the reader; example graphs (sums of sin x with higher harmonics) illustrate how combining harmonics behaves and leads into Fourier-type behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discontinuities and vertical asymptotes of tan and cot
rubrics_metrics.description: y = tan x is not defined at x = (2k+1)·90° and has vertical asymptotes there; y = cot x is not defined at x = k·180° and has vertical asymptotes at those points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: as x approaches the undefined angles, tangent values grow without bound; figure references show the graphs approaching asymptotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concavity (convexity) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f(x) is concave up (convex) on [a,b] if the graph of f lies under the line connecting any two points on the graph; concave down if it lies above that line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric intuition: concave up looks like a bowl that holds water, concave down like a bowl that spills water. Formal definition in terms of any a1 < x < b1 in [a,b].

rubrics_metrics.name: Jensen's inequality (statement and implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is concave up on [a,b] and λ1,...,λn are nonnegative with sum 1 then λ1 f(x1)+...+λn f(xn) ≥ f(λ1 x1+...+λn xn). If f is concave down the inequality is reversed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: output of convex function at weighted average is ≤ weighted average of outputs. Applications: derive inequalities involving sums of sin or tan on triangle angles; connection to second derivative for calculus-literate readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convexity applications to trigonometric sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Using convexity (Jensen), y = sin x is concave down on 0°≤x≤180°, so sin A + sin B + sin C ≤ 3·(sin((A+B+C)/3)) = 3·sin 60° = 3√3/2 for triangle angles; similarly tan is concave up on 0°≤x<90° leading to tan A + tan B + tan C ≥ 3√3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text provides which triangle problems this method helps and notes the authors avoid heavy functional analysis in solutions but still demonstrate the technique in select problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extended law of sines (a/sin A = 2R)
rubrics_metrics.description: In triangle ABC with circumradius R, a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C = 2R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation via right-triangle geometry and midpoint of chord; geometric meaning for the common ratio a/sin A. Alternate derivation by extending radii is noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of sines
rubrics_metrics.description: sin A / a = sin B / b = sin C / c or equivalently a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly to relate side ratios and angles; applied to prove angle-bisector theorem and other triangle constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angle-bisector theorem via law of sines
rubrics_metrics.description: If AD bisects angle A in triangle ABC and D is on BC, then |AB|/|AC| = |BD|/|CD|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: apply law of sines in triangles ABD and ACD and equate appropriate sines; text also mentions external bisector generalization left to reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangle area formula using a side and included angle
rubrics_metrics.description: Area [ABC] = (1/2)·ab·sin C (equivalently (1/2)·bc·sin A = (1/2)·ca·sin B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from dropping perpendicular from a vertex; used to relate areas in quadrilaterals and in proofs like Ptolemy and Brahmagupta.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area of quadrilateral via diagonals and intersection angle
rubrics_metrics.description: For quadrilateral ABCD with diagonals AC and BD meeting at P, [ABCD] = (1/2)·|AC|·|BD|·sin ∠APB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by splitting quadrilateral into two triangles sharing AC and summing areas; used in area-based proofs of Ptolemy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ptolemy's theorem for cyclic quadrilaterals
rubrics_metrics.description: In a convex cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, |AC|·|BD| = |AB|·|CD| + |AD|·|BC|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof provided via areas and a reflection construction producing an isosceles trapezoid; guidance describes expressing products of sides in terms of areas and sine of intersection angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cyclic quadrilateral geometry to derive trigonometric identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometric constructions (e.g., regular heptagon and Ptolemy) can produce trigonometric equalities such as csc(180°/7) = csc(360°/7) + csc(540°/7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two approaches provided: algebraic using angle addition formulas and geometric via cyclic polygons and Ptolemy; demonstrates interplay of geometry and trig identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: SSA (side-side-angle) ambiguity explained by sin equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Because sin α = sin β when α + β = 180°, SSA information can lead to two possible triangle configurations (two possible angles with same sine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show how area and side-length constraints produce two possible angle measures (e.g., A = 60° or 120°) or impossibility when sine exceeds 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of injective/surjective/bijective for trig functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sine and cosine map angles to [-1,1] (surjective onto that interval); sine is bijection from [-90°,90°] to [-1,1]; cosine is bijection from [0°,180°] to [-1,1]; tangent is bijection from (-90°,90°) to R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text emphasizes domain restrictions to obtain one-to-one correspondences and motivates definitions of inverse functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse trig functions: ranges and notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Define arcsin, arccos, arctan, arccot with specific principal value ranges: arcsin: [-90°,90°], arccos: [0°,180°], arctan: (-90°,90°), arccot: (-90°,90°] \ {0°}. Note arcsin x is not 1/sin x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graphical behavior is discussed; arctan has horizontal asymptotes y=±90° and arccot pieces are asymptotic to y=0; readers are invited to sketch compositions like sin(arcsin x) and arcsin(sin x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigonometric substitution for sequences and recurrences
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitute x_n = tan α_n (with α_n in principal range) to convert Möbius-type recursions like x_{n+1} = (1 + x_n)/(1 − x_n) into angular addition α_{n+1} = 45° + α_n (mod 180°), revealing periodicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: sequence x_{n+1} = (1 + x_n)/(1 − x_n) has period 4 because α increases by 45° each step; general technique: use bijectivity of tan on (-90°,90°).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigeonhole principle with tangents for inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent real numbers as tan x_k with x_k in (-90°,90°) and partition that interval into four 45°-wide subintervals; among five numbers two x_i,x_j lie in same subinterval implying |(a−b)/(1+ab)| < 1 and hence |ab+1| > |a−b|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique combines trigonometric parametrization with pigeonhole to derive nontrivial algebraic inequalities; concrete example given for five numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy–Schwarz and trig substitution in optimization problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Use trigonometric parametrizations (e.g., set z = sin^2 a, x = cos^2 a cos^2 b, y = cos^2 a sin^2 b) to convert rational expressions into forms amenable to inequalities such as Cauchy–Schwarz or algebraic inequalities (x^2+y^2 ≥ 2xy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: minimizing 1/x + 4/y + 9/z under x+y+z=1; authors show a trig-substitution solution that reduces to establishing lower bounds and identifying equality cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ceva's theorem (trigonometric and segment-product forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three cevians AD, BE, CF of triangle ABC are concurrent iff (trig form) (sin ∠ABE / sin ∠DAB)·(sin ∠BCF / sin ∠EBC)·(sin ∠CAD / sin ∠FCA) = 1, equivalently (length form) (AF/FB)·(BD/DC)·(CE/EA) = 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text shows implications (1)⇒(2)⇒(3)⇒(1) via law of sines; mentions medians, altitudes and angle bisectors as concurrent examples (centroid, orthocenter, incenter) and generalizations including external bisectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Menelaus's theorem (collinearity criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given triangle ABC and points F on BC, G on CA, H on AB, points F,G,H are collinear iff (AH/HB)·(BF/FC)·(CG/GA) = 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation uses law of sines applied to triangles formed by the transversal; text notes utility in synthetic geometry though not elaborated further in trig-focused problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Cosines (SAS and SSS forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: In triangle ABC, b^2 = c^2 + a^2 − 2ca cos B, and equivalently cos B = (c^2 + a^2 − b^2)/(2ca).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation by dropping perpendiculars and analyzing right triangles; law of cosines used for computing side lengths (SAS) or computing cosine from side lengths (SSS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stewart's theorem (relation for cevian lengths)
rubrics_metrics.description: For triangle ABC and point D on BC, |AB|^2·|CD| + |AC|^2·|BD| = |BC|(|AD|^2 + |BD|·|CD|).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof provided by applying law of cosines to triangles ABD and ACD and eliminating cos terms; median formula emerges as a special case when D is midpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brahmagupta's formula for cyclic quadrilateral area
rubrics_metrics.description: For convex cyclic quadrilateral with side lengths a,b,c,d and semiperimeter s, area [ABCD] = √((s−a)(s−b)(s−c)(s−d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses expression for sin B from law of cosines with cyclic condition B + D = 180° and area decomposition into two triangles; Heron's formula is a degenerate special case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heron's formula for triangle area
rubrics_metrics.description: Area of triangle with sides a,b,c and semiperimeter s = (a+b+c)/2 is [ABC] = √(s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as degenerate case of Brahmagupta when one diagonal length tends to zero (triangle viewed as cyclic quadrilateral with one side zero); readers encouraged to derive independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brocard point existence and Brocard angle relations
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a unique interior point P of triangle ABC such that ∠PAB = ∠PBC = ∠PCA (a Brocard point). Its defining property is that the circumcircle of certain triangles through P is tangent at a vertex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction approach: locate centers of circles tangent at vertices and passing through other vertices; Brocard points are isogonal conjugates. Also provide formulas: tan α = 4[ABC]/(a^2 + b^2 + c^2) and csc^2 α = csc^2 A + csc^2 B + csc^2 C, with derivations using law of cosines and area relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vector representation in plane (directed segments)
rubrics_metrics.description: For points A=(x1,y1) and B=(x2,y2), define vector AB = [x2 − x1, y2 − y1]. Vector addition composes displacements (AB + BC = AC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduces directed segments and coordinate computations with concrete numeric example; used to transition geometric problems into coordinate/vector methods.
